When the advertising message contains sufficiently precise elements about the object, its qualities, conditions or advantages, it becomes part of the offer and radiates obligational effects over the consumer relationship, binding the supplier to the content conveyed <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 140-142)</2>.

In the consumer protection system, the marketing message is no longer legally indifferent and functions as a source of obligation whenever, through its degree of precision and its capacity to shape expectations, it makes up the content of the offer addressed to the consumer <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 144)</2>.

Unlawfulness may arise whenever the message, even if partially true, is capable of leading the consumer into error, including by omission, ambiguity, relevant incompleteness or by the very form in which the content is presented <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 167)</2>.

Deceptiveness may emerge, for example, when the real price is not shown clearly, when charges are relegated to a visually insignificant position or when the decisive information is technically included but functionally hidden in the context of the piece <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 168)</2>.

This occurs because, in markets marked by lean, opaque or incomplete adhesion contracts, the marketing message often anticipates, completes and densifies the understanding the consumer forms about the utility, the qualities and the mode of enjoyment of the object offered, becoming a relevant element in the construction of their legitimate expectation <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 142)</2>.

The more eloquent, precise and guiding the message, the greater its capacity to generate trust worthy of protection and, therefore, the greater its binding force as well <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 42)</2>.

Marketing communication takes part in manufacturing the very disposition to contract by inflating needs, organizing desires and presenting, at the same time, the path to their satisfaction, leading the consumer to the culminating moment of adhesion <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 91])</2>.

This inseparability is accentuated because the marketing message usually brings together, in a single arrangement, concrete offers, fanciful promises and accessory advantages integrated into a marketing mix, in such a way that the social action of advertisers becomes a source of duties and obligations <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 95])</2>.

It may also arise in hybrid, disguised arrangements or ones embedded in apparently neutral media, in which the commercial message infiltrates narrative contexts that reduce the consumer's critical vigilance and intensify their vulnerability to inducement <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 123-125])</2>.

This happens when marketing communication presents itself as entertainment, reporting or neutral recommendation, although in practice it works as a vector of commercial steering, which is why the outlet's responsibility lies precisely in not allowing advertising to be confused with editorial content <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 123-125])</2>.

Examining interactive narratives and games, Lesnovski observes that this kind of experience is organized by permanent tensions between choice and control, illusion and simulation, action and identity, culminating in the production of an “experience of controlled freedom”, in which the user's action always occurs in relation to a structure that precedes and conditions it <1>Lesnovski</1><2>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 7)</2>.

The point becomes even more precise when the author notes that the one who interacts is foreseen in the structure itself and that the interactive experience is formed in the coupling between the system's stimuli and the participant's responses, without the latter ceasing to act, but also without acting outside the environment that organizes them <1>Lesnovski</1><2>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 16; p. 18)</2>.

Along similar lines, in addressing systems of reward and punishment, Lesnovski shows that they do not operate merely as episodic reactions to isolated conduct, but as forms of control by the system over free and potentially deviant actions, keeping the experience flowing, avoiding aporias and leading the one who interacts back to the structurally foreseen path <1>Lesnovski</1><2>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 79-80)</2>.

In The author maintains that interactive narrative should be read neither as the interactor's full freedom nor as pure deception, but as a field of tensions in which text, system and participant are articulated in variable relations of choice, control, illusion, simulation, action and identity <1>Lesnovski</1><2>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 7)</2>.

Her argument is especially relevant in stating that the interactive experience creates a “controlled freedom”, in which the user's action takes place within a structure that foresees them and offers them margins of intervention without ever relinquishing command over the conditions of possibility of the experience itself <1>Lesnovski</1><2>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 7; p. 18)</2>.

The author also examines the function of reward and punishment systems as forms of control by the computational system over the free and potentially uncontrolled actions of the interactor, observing that such mechanisms serve not only to reward or punish on a one-off basis, but to keep the experience in flow, avoid excessive deviations and steer the interaction back onto paths intelligible to the system itself <1>Lesnovski</1><2>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 79-80)</2>.

When there is imbalance, however, the experience itself may degenerate into frustration or punishment, which reveals the delicacy of the arrangement between felt freedom and structural limitation <1>Lesnovski</1><2>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 175)</2>.

The rereading of private law in light of human dignity has long since broken with the narrow view that confined the legal problem to the patrimonial value of the affected good, demanding attention to the existential projections of the person in the social world <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 10; p. 17)</2>.

The civil protection of personality reaches precisely the way the person is projected, recognized and situated in the social milieu, which is why reputation, honor and identity receive protection not because they are mere inner feelings, but because they make up objective relational dimensions of the person's life <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 71; p. 211)</2>.

The protection of identity covers not only formal signs, but the faithful presentation of the person in their singularity, preventing compressions, falsifications and fixations produced by third parties <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 155-156; p. 216)</2>.

The rereading of private law in light of human dignity breaks precisely with the excessively patrimonialist outlook that confined the legal problem to the economic value of the affected good, demanding attention also to the existential projections of the person in the social world <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 10)</2>.

The advantage of this formulation lies precisely in preventing the protection of the person from depending on sentimental proof or on dramatization of the harm, focusing instead on the legally protected projection that was violated <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 17)</2>.

Reputation and honor receive their own legal protection: not because they represent mere inner feelings, but because they make up objective relational dimensions of the person's life, socially relevant and normatively protected <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 71)</2>.

This conclusion is reinforced when personal identity is treated not as merely formal data, but as protection of the right to be oneself in social space, that is, of respect for the traits, experiences, convictions and marks that singularize the person before others <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 211)</2>.

When data and records begin to be used to fix representations of the individual, there is a risk, relevant to civil law, of compressing their singularity and of affecting the way they will be apprehended, treated and positioned in the social world <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 155-156)</2>.
